stimulus.text: The 1771 map by Thomas Hutchins marks the village of Cahokia on the Mississippi River, near present-day St. Louis. The pre-contact city of Cahokia stood in this same river valley centuries earlier. Archaeologists who have mapped Cahokia describe a city of mounds, plazas, and a wooden palisade. Trade goods from far away reached the city: copper from the Great Lakes and shells from the Gulf Coast.
stimulus.source_note: Map from the shared image pool; Thomas Hutchins (1771), public domain. Archaeological description paraphrased from standard accounts of Cahokia.

stem: This 1771 map marks Cahokia on the Mississippi River, near present-day St. Louis. Mississippian chiefdoms like Cahokia built their towns in the river valleys of the Southeast and Midwest. Which factor best explains this location pattern?

options.text: River valleys provided fertile floodplain soils for the maize surpluses chiefdoms depended on.
The Mexica Empire in central Mexico had already claimed all the uplands.
Spanish officials ordered Native towns to be built along rivers for easier control.
Rivers were the only source of drinking water anywhere in North America.

instruction: Pick one option from the stimulus and stem only. Do not open the question file.
